source.title: Algorithmic Semi-algebraic Geometry and Topology -- Recent Progress and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let S be a semi-algebraic subset of R^k defined by s polynomials whose degrees are at most d. Does there exist an algorithm for computing the entire sequence of Betti numbers of S whose running time is single-exponential in k? The paper explains that single-exponential-time algorithms are known for computing only the first ℓ Betti numbers when ℓ is fixed, and asks whether those ideas can be extended to compute all Betti numbers of an arbitrary semi-algebraic set.
accepted.context_brief: Single-exponential algorithms for all Betti numbers

evidence.quote:
Computing Betti Numbers in Single Exponential Time ? Suppose S ⊂ R^k is a semi-
algebraic set defined in terms of s polynomials, of degrees bounded by d. One of
the most fundamental open questions in algorithmic semi-algebraic geometry, is
whether there exists a single exponential (in k) time algorithm for computing the
Betti numbers of S. The best we can do so far is summarized in Theorem 6.10
which gives the existence of single exponential time algorithms for computing the
first ℓ Betti numbers of S for any constant ℓ. A big challenge is to extend these
ideas to design an algorithm for computing all the Betti numbers of S.

accepted.question_text: Is there a complexity-theoretic hardness explanation for why the middle Betti numbers of a semi-algebraic set seem harder to compute than the lowest Betti numbers, the highest Betti numbers, or the Euler–Poincaré characteristic? More specifically, can one identify a complexity-theoretic analogue of the geometric phenomenon in which middle Betti numbers carry essentially all of the information, thereby explaining the observed difficulty of computing them?

evidence.quote:
Are the Middle Betti Numbers Harder to Compute ? From the algorithm design per-
spective it seems that computing the lowest (as well as the highest) Betti numbers
of semi-algebraic sets, as well the Euler-Poincar´e characteristic of semi-algebraic
sets, are easier than computing the "middle" Betti numbers. Is there a complexity-
theoretic hardness result that would justify this fact? In certain mathematical
contexts (for instance, the topology of smooth projective complex varieties) the
middle Betti numbers contain all the information. Is there a complexity-theoretic
analogue of this phenomenon that would justify our experience that certain Betti
numbers are harder to compute than the others?

accepted.question_text: Consider a semi-algebraic set in R^k defined by ℓ quadratic inequalities. Is there an algorithm for counting its connected components with complexity k^{O(ℓ)}, or even k^{O(ℓ^2)}, instead of relying on the currently known more expensive general method? The problem is motivated by the fact that emptiness testing, sample-point computation, and Euler–Poincaré characteristic computation for this quadratic setting already admit algorithms with complexity k^{O(ℓ)}, but counting connected components still lacks an equally efficient algorithm.

accepted.question_text: For a general semi-algebraic set, can roadmap algorithms for testing connectivity be improved so that the exponent in their complexity drops from O(k^2) to O(k)? Equivalently, can testing connectivity be made asymptotically as efficient as emptiness testing for general semi-algebraic sets by obtaining a substantially better complexity bound for roadmap construction?
